title: Mental Health First Aid Self-Reflection Program
short: Understand your mental health, notice the signs, and learn how to support yourself and others.
intro: Four short phases you work through in order. Each one has three lessons, three short videos, one reflection activity and a five-question quiz. Go at your own pace.
learn: What mental health is and how it shows up in your body, thoughts and habits
How to spot early changes in yourself and others
Why feelings get hidden, and safer ways to express them
How to check in with someone and connect them to support
disclaimer: This program is educational. It isn't a diagnosis, a treatment, or an accredited Mental Health First Aid course.

phases.title: How's Your Head, Really?
phases.description: Learn what mental health really means and how it shows up in your body, thoughts, and habits. Start noticing what supports your wellbeing and what makes things harder.
objectives: Describe mental health as part of whole-person health
Place yourself on the mental health continuum
Name things that support and strain your wellbeing

lessons.title: Mental Health Isn't Just Mental
lessons.intro: Mental health is how we think, feel and act. It affects how we handle stress, connect with people and make choices. And it doesn't stay in your head.

sections.h: It shows up in three places
p: When your mental health shifts, you'll usually notice it somewhere first:
list: Your body: sleep, energy, appetite, tension, headaches
Your thoughts: focus, worry, the way you talk to yourself
Your habits: how you spend time, who you see, how you switch off

p: Just like physical health, everyone has mental health. It isn't the same as having a mental illness. It changes over time, with good stretches and harder ones.

lessons.example: During a busy month at work, Sam sleeps badly, skips the gym and snaps at his housemate. None of that makes him a bad person. It's his mental health showing up in his body and habits.
lessons.takeaway: Mental health is part of your overall health. Noticing it in your body and habits is the first skill.

lessons.title: Okay vs Not Okay — What's the Line?
lessons.intro: There isn't a single line between okay and not okay. It's more useful to think of a continuum that we all move along.

p: People often describe four broad zones. Moving between them is normal.
list: Thriving: feeling like yourself, coping well
Coping: some stress, but managing
Struggling: things feel harder and it's starting to affect daily life
Unwell: distress is high and daily life is significantly affected

p: A bad day on its own isn't a warning sign. Context matters. Pay closer attention when:
list: Changes last for more than a couple of weeks
They affect work, study, relationships or sleep
You or others feel you're not yourself

p: If distress is persistent, getting worse, or getting in the way of daily life, talk to a GP or mental health professional. You don't need to wait until things are severe.

lessons.example: Priya feels nervous before a big exam. That's a normal reaction. If she'd felt flat and unable to concentrate for weeks, that would be worth checking in about.
lessons.takeaway: Look for changes that last, and that affect daily life. Getting support early is a sensible step, not an overreaction.

lessons.title: What Shapes the Storm?
lessons.intro: Many things influence mental health. Some make things harder. Others help protect us. Knowing your own mix helps you look after yourself.

sections.h: Things that can make it harder
list: Ongoing stress at work, study or home
Big changes, like a move, loss or breakup
Loneliness or feeling disconnected
Poor sleep or physical illness
Difficult past experiences
Supportive relationships
Regular sleep and movement
Activities that feel meaningful
Skills for handling stress
Knowing where to get help

p: These factors shift the odds. They don't decide outcomes. Someone with lots of support can still struggle, and that's not a personal failure.

lessons.example: After moving cities, Leah has fewer friends nearby and works long hours. Joining a weekend walking group gives her connection and movement, two protective factors at once.
lessons.takeaway: Notice what strains your wellbeing and what supports it. Small protective habits add up.

activity.title: What Does Good Mental Health Feel Like to You?
activity.purpose: Build a picture of what feeling like yourself looks like, so you can notice when things change.
activity.instructions: Answer as much or as little as you like. You can skip any question and come back later.

prompts.q: When you're feeling at your best, what do you notice in your body, thoughts and energy?
What everyday things help you feel like yourself?
What tends to make things harder for you?
What's one small thing you could do this week to look after your wellbeing?

questions.q: Which statement best describes mental health?
options: How we think, feel and act, and it affects our body and habits too
questions.explain: Everyone has mental health. It covers thoughts, feelings and behaviour, and it shows up in the body and in habits.

questions.q: A person's mental health can move along a continuum, from thriving to struggling, over time.
questions.explain: Moving along the continuum is normal. Where someone sits can change with circumstances.

questions.q: Which is most worth paying attention to?
options: Feeling unlike yourself for several weeks, and it's affecting daily life
Being tired after a long trip
questions.explain: Changes that last and affect daily life matter more than one-off reactions to normal events.

questions.q: Which of these is a protective factor?
questions.explain: Supportive relationships help protect wellbeing. The others tend to make things harder.

questions.q: If someone has plenty of protective factors, they can't experience mental health difficulties.
questions.explain: Protective factors shift the odds but don't guarantee anything. Anyone can struggle.

phases.title: Check Yourself, Kindly
phases.description: Learn to spot changes in your mood, energy, behaviour, and physical wellbeing. Build awareness of stress signals and recognise when you may need additional support.
objectives: Notice quieter changes in mood and behaviour
Choose a healthy response instead of coping alone

lessons.title: Your Body Is a Messenger
lessons.intro: Stress often reaches the body before we've named it. Learning your body's signals gives you an early heads-up.

list: Tight shoulders, neck or jaw
Headaches or an upset stomach
A racing heart or shallow breathing
Feeling tired even after rest
Changes in sleep or appetite

p: These signs can also have physical causes. If they keep happening, see a GP. It's not either mind or body.
Pause. Notice your jaw, shoulders and breathing. Ask yourself: what is my body telling me right now?

lessons.example: Every Sunday night, Jordan gets a tight chest and can't sleep. Noticing the pattern helps him link it to Monday meetings and plan for them.
lessons.takeaway: Your body often signals stress first. Notice the pattern, and get physical symptoms checked if they persist.

lessons.title: Not All Red Flags Are Loud
lessons.intro: Some changes are obvious. Many are quiet and easy to explain away.

list: Pulling back from people or things you enjoy
Getting irritated more easily
Putting things off more than usual
Using screens, food or alcohol to switch off
Feeling flat rather than sad

p: One quiet weekend means nothing. A shift from your usual self that sticks around is worth noticing.

lessons.example: Mia used to message friends daily. Over a month she's stopped replying and spends evenings scrolling. Nothing dramatic happened, but the change is real.
lessons.takeaway: Compare yourself to your usual self. Quiet changes that last deserve attention.

lessons.title: The Cost of Coping Alone
lessons.intro: Many of us try to handle things on our own. It can feel easier, but it often makes things harder over time.

list: Not wanting to be a burden
Thinking others have it worse
Not knowing what to say
Worrying about being judged

p: Problems can grow quietly, and isolation can make everything feel heavier.

list: Name what's going on, even just to yourself
Tell someone you trust
Make one small change, like a walk or earlier night
See a GP or mental health professional if things persist or get worse

lessons.example: After weeks of feeling exhausted, Ali tells his sister. She helps him book a GP appointment he'd been putting off.
lessons.takeaway: You don't have to handle everything alone. Reaching out early is a strength.

activity.title: When My Mind Speaks Through My Body
activity.purpose: Learn your personal early signals so you can respond sooner.
activity.instructions: Think about a recent stressful time. Keep it general if you prefer. You don't need to describe the situation.

prompts.q: Where did you feel it in your body?
What other changes did you notice, in sleep, appetite, energy or habits?
What's one early signal you'd like to notice sooner?

questions.q: Which can be a physical sign of stress?
questions.explain: Muscle tension in the shoulders and jaw is a common physical stress signal.

questions.q: Physical symptoms like headaches always have a mental health cause.
questions.explain: They can have physical causes too. If they persist, check with a GP.

questions.q: Which quiet change might suggest someone is struggling?
options: Pulling back from things they used to enjoy
questions.explain: Withdrawing from things someone usually enjoys is a common quiet change.

questions.q: What's most helpful when looking at warning signs?
options: Look for changes from usual and patterns over time
questions.explain: Patterns and changes from someone's usual self tell you more than any single moment.

questions.q: You've felt flat and exhausted for three weeks and it's affecting work. What's a healthy next step?
options: Talk to someone you trust and consider seeing a GP
Wait for it to pass on its own
questions.explain: When changes last and affect daily life, talking to someone and seeing a GP are sensible steps.

phases.title: Safe to Feel, Safe to Speak
phases.description: Understand why people hide their emotions and learn how to recognise, explore, and express feelings more safely.
objectives: Practise naming and sharing feelings safely

lessons.title: Why It's Hard to Talk About It
lessons.intro: If talking about feelings feels hard, you're in good company. There are real reasons it's difficult.

list: Fear of being judged or seen as weak
Not having the words for what you feel
Past experiences of being brushed off
Family or cultural norms about privacy
Not wanting to worry people

p: They're often ways of protecting yourself. Understanding them is the first step to choosing when they still serve you.

lessons.example: Growing up, Dev learned that his family 'didn't talk about that stuff'. As an adult, he finds it easier to start with a friend outside the family.
lessons.takeaway: Finding it hard to talk is common and understandable. You can start small.

lessons.title: The Mask We Wear
lessons.intro: Emotional masking means appearing fine on the outside while feeling something different inside.

list: To keep things running at work or home
To protect others from worry
To avoid questions we're not ready for

p: Masking for a long time can be exhausting. It also means others can't offer support, because they don't know you need it.
Sometimes a mask helps you get through a moment. It's worth noticing when it has become the default everywhere.

lessons.example: Rosa is the 'funny one' in her team. Lately the jokes feel like hard work, and she's tired by lunchtime.
lessons.takeaway: Notice where you wear a mask and what it costs you. Choose one safe place to take it off.

lessons.title: You Deserve to Speak
lessons.intro: Expressing feelings safely is a skill you can build, a little at a time.

p: 'Fine' and 'stressed' cover a lot. Try being more specific: tired, flat, on edge, lonely, overwhelmed, hopeful, relieved.
Self-compassion means speaking to yourself the way you'd speak to a good friend. It isn't letting yourself off the hook. It makes change easier.

sections.h: Choose who, when and how much
list: Pick someone who has been safe before
Choose a calm time
You decide how much to share
A simple start: "I've been finding things hard lately."

lessons.example: Instead of 'I'm fine', Tom tells his partner, 'I'm feeling flat and I'm not sure why.' It opens a conversation without pressure to explain everything.
lessons.takeaway: Asking for help isn't a burden. Naming a feeling is a good first step.

activity.title: What Are You Really Feeling?
activity.purpose: Practise naming feelings more precisely and notice what you tend to hide.
activity.instructions: There are no right answers. Share only what feels comfortable.

prompts.q: Which words describe how you've felt this week?
Is there a feeling you tend to hide? What makes it hard to show?
Who is someone you feel safe being honest with? (No names needed.)
Write one kind sentence to yourself about what you're feeling.

questions.q: What is emotional masking?
options: Hiding how you really feel behind an 'I'm fine'
Wearing a face mask when unwell
Always saying exactly what you feel
questions.explain: Masking means appearing fine on the outside while feeling something different inside.

questions.q: Fear of being judged is a common reason people don't talk about how they feel.
questions.explain: Fear of judgement is one of the most common barriers to speaking up.

questions.q: Which builds emotional awareness?
questions.explain: Naming specific feelings helps you understand them and talk about them.

questions.q: Self-compassion means:
options: Speaking to yourself with the kindness you'd show a friend
questions.explain: Self-compassion is treating yourself with the same kindness you'd offer someone you care about.

questions.q: Asking for help means you're a burden.
questions.explain: Asking for help is a normal, healthy step. Most people want to help the people they care about.

phases.title: Mental Health First Aid
phases.description: Learn to recognise when someone may be struggling, check in with care, maintain appropriate boundaries, and help connect people to suitable support.
objectives: Notice when someone may be struggling
Know your role and your limits
Know where to direct people for help

lessons.title: Signs That Go Unspoken
lessons.intro: People rarely announce that they're struggling. Often the signs are changes you notice over time.

list: Withdrawing from friends, family or activities
Changes in mood, like irritability or seeming flat
Changes in sleep, appetite or appearance
Trouble keeping up at work or study
Saying they feel hopeless, trapped or like a burden

p: No single sign proves anything. Your job isn't to work out what's wrong. It's to notice a change and check in.

sections.h: If someone is in immediate danger
p: If someone talks about ending their life or you think they're in immediate danger, call 000. Stay with them if it's safe to do so.

lessons.example: Kim's colleague has been missing deadlines, eating lunch alone and once said 'what's the point'. Kim doesn't know what's going on, but decides to check in.
lessons.takeaway: Notice changes, consider context, and check in. You don't need to have answers.

lessons.title: How to Ask Without Making It Weird
lessons.intro: Checking in doesn't need a script. A caring, simple question goes a long way.

list: Pick a private, unhurried time
Put your phone away
Be ready to listen more than talk
"I've noticed you seem quieter lately. How are you going?"
"You haven't seemed yourself. Want to grab a walk?"
"I'm here if you ever want to talk."
Don't rush to fix or give advice
Reflect back what you hear
It's okay if they don't want to talk. Leave the door open and follow up later
If you're worried about their safety, it's okay to ask them directly

lessons.example: Instead of 'What's wrong with you?', Ben says, 'You've seemed stressed lately. I'm around if you want to talk.' His friend opens up a few days later.
lessons.takeaway: Start with what you've noticed, listen without judging, and keep the door open.

lessons.title: Be the Bridge, Not the Fix
lessons.intro: Your role is to support and connect, not to be someone's therapist.

list: Listens and takes them seriously
Encourages professional support, like a GP or psychologist
Shares crisis lines if things are serious
Follows up later
You can't fix someone's mental health for them
Don't promise to keep secrets if someone's safety is at risk
Look after your own wellbeing too
Ask for help yourself if supporting someone feels heavy

p: In an emergency, call 000. For 24/7 crisis support in Australia, Lifeline is on 13 11 14. A GP is a good first step for ongoing support.

lessons.example: Sara listens to her friend, helps her book a GP appointment and checks in after. She also tells her own partner she needs a quiet night to recharge.
lessons.takeaway: Support, connect and follow up. Looking after yourself is part of the role. This program doesn't make you an accredited first aider.

activity.title: Your Role in Someone's Mental Health Journey
activity.purpose: Plan how you might support someone, while respecting your own limits.
activity.instructions: Think of someone you care about, or imagine a scenario. No names or personal details needed.

prompts.q: What changes might tell you this person is struggling?
How would you start the conversation? Write your opening line.
What support could you point them towards?
What are your limits, and how will you look after yourself?

questions.q: Which might suggest someone is struggling?
options: Withdrawing from friends and changes in their usual behaviour
Being quiet in a single meeting
questions.explain: Lasting changes in behaviour and connection are more meaningful than one-off moments.

questions.q: Which is a good way to start a check-in?
options: "I've noticed you seem quieter lately. How are you going?"
Bring it up in front of the group
questions.explain: Start privately with what you've noticed, and ask an open question.

questions.q: As a support person, your role is to diagnose and fix the problem.
questions.explain: Your role is to be a bridge: listen, support and connect them to professional help.

questions.q: A friend says they've felt hopeless for weeks. What's a helpful step?
options: Tell them everyone feels that way
Listen, and encourage them to see a GP or mental health professional
Promise to keep it secret no matter what
questions.explain: Listening and encouraging professional support is helpful. Don't promise secrecy if their safety may be at risk.

questions.q: If someone is in immediate danger in Australia, you should:
options: Wait and see how they are tomorrow
questions.explain: For immediate danger, call 000.
